title: CVIP Malta | Owner's CAS/CAP for Bunkering Calls and Docking
description: CVIP in Malta: an owner's CAS/CAP-style programme staged across bunkering stops at Hurd's Bank, Freeport calls and Grand Harbour dockings, with one record.
h1: Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme in Malta: an owner's condition assessment staged across bunkering stops, Freeport calls and Grand Harbour dockings
intro: Ships stop at Malta for fuel, orders, crew changes, transhipment and repair, and many of the managers who run them work on the island because of its flag. CVIP, our Comprehensive Vessel Inspection Programme, uses those stops to build a measured condition record. Managers on the island frequently put the request as an owner's CAS or owner's CAP, meaning the depth of those official schemes brought to bear for the owner's own purposes, with no class involvement. Its baseline and the visits that follow, at the offshore anchorages, at Marsaxlokk or in a Grand Harbour dock, feed one trend record. The team flies in from India each time.

highlights.h: A bunkering stop becomes a programme visit
highlights.p: Ships taking fuel at Hurd's Bank or the other designated areas lie at anchor with no cargo work under way. A visit by launch in that time covers machinery under load, deck fittings and prepared tanks, without adding a port call to the voyage.

highlights.h: Managers and dock on one island
highlights.p: With many Malta-flag managers working from the island and Palumbo Malta Shipyard in Grand Harbour, the superintendent can attend the docking visit, settle priorities with the team in person and see the findings before the ship leaves the yard.

The offshore areas are open to the weather, and a sea state that suits bunkering can still rule out a safe transfer with equipment. Programme visits there carry modules that can move to the next stop, while tank and dock work is kept for sheltered settings.

sections.h: Can a ship be assessed during a bunkering stop off Malta?
p: Partly, and usefully. A ship at Hurd's Bank or another of the designated anchorage and bunkering areas is idle apart from the bunker transfer, and her machinery is often running on port load. The team boards by a launch the agent books, agrees with the master which spaces are released and how the visit fits around the bunkering operation, and works through a list fixed in the programme plan.

What fits is set by time, weather and the bunkering itself. Engine-room machinery and switchboards, deck plating and fittings, hatch covers on dry cargo ships, scrubber lines and ballast tanks the crew has ventilated are typical. Work near the bunker manifold waits until the transfer is complete, and spaces that need lengthy preparation are left for the Freeport, a terminal or the shipyard. A visit cut short by the weather loses nothing from the record; the remaining items move to the next stop on the plan, and the visit report says so.

sections.h: Malta-flag managers with ships trading worldwide
p: Europe's largest ship register is administered by Transport Malta's Merchant Shipping Directorate, and the flag has drawn many owning and ship-management companies to set up on the island. Their ships trade everywhere, so a programme set up in Malta does not have to take all its visits there. The plan is agreed with the technical department on the island, and visits are made wherever each ship stops long enough, with Malta stops used whenever the voyage brings the ship past.

The flag does not change the measurement work itself. Statutory surveys of Malta-flag ships are carried out by classification societies acting as recognised organisations, and each society sets the thickness measurement its surveys require. The programme sits beside that framework, giving the manager a record that is the owner's own and is kept in one format whichever society classes the ship. For a manager whose fleet is spread across several societies, that consistency is often the reason for starting a programme.

sections.h: The Grand Harbour docking as the programme's checkpoint
p: Palumbo Malta Shipyard, in the old dock area at Cospicua, handles anything from a ferry or offshore vessel to a large cruise ship or tanker. For a ship in a Malta programme, a docking there is the visit that sees everything: the dry bottom, sea chests and rudder, cargo and ballast tanks once gas-freed, and staging in the larger spaces. A pre-docking round on an earlier stop gives the yard its renewal outline; after repairs, renewed areas are measured again so the trend continues from the new steel.

Cruise ships bring their own emphasis. Refurbishment periods at the yard combine hull items with exhaust gas cleaning and exhaust system work, and the programme uses them to gauge scrubber discharge lines and shell outlets with the hull dry, to survey hot surfaces and their insulation with a thermal camera, and to read machinery that seldom stops in service. Each of those becomes a fixed point in the cruise ship's record, measured again on turnaround days at the Valletta Cruise Port.

sections.h: Owner's CAS, owner's CAP and what the Malta flag still requires
p: Malta-based managers use the names owner's CAS and owner's CAP for a reason: they want the depth those schemes are known for, applied when their own decisions need it. CVIP supplies it through a survey plan taken from the drawings and survey history, close-up examination, gauging at fixed positions, coatings graded GOOD, FAIR or POOR, machinery read while running, and one condition report in which every finding carries a grade.

What belongs to the official bodies stays with them. Where the IMO Condition Assessment Scheme applies to an older tanker, the Statement of Compliance comes from the flag Administration after review of the recognised organisation's report; a CAP rating comes from the classification society that carried out the CAP survey. CVIP produces neither. A charterer who names the class CAP should receive it from the society, with the programme's readings telling the owner beforehand where the ship probably stands.

Readings taken in a Malta programme are likewise the owner's evidence rather than class gauging. A society credits thickness measurement to a survey solely from firms it has approved under IACS UR Z17. Atlantis is still working towards that approval with Lloyd's Register, ABS and DNV; until one of them issues a certificate, CVIP results inform the owner's steel, docking, chartering and sale decisions and are not offered for credit to any class survey.

sections.h: Planning: Luqa flights, Schengen visas and late notice of bunkering calls
p: Malta International Airport at Luqa lies close to both Grand Harbour and Marsaxlokk, and because Malta belongs to Schengen, each technician travelling from India carries a Schengen visa issued before departure. Dockings at the shipyard are booked well ahead and suit visa timing. Bunkering stops are confirmed later, so the programme plan identifies likely Malta stops from the voyage pattern and keeps visas valid across them; the same visa period can also cover a fleet ship calling in Sicily or southern Italy.

Ahead of the baseline we need the hull drawings with as-built scantlings, the gauging report from the last survey, class status and outstanding items, the planned maintenance equipment list and any earlier vibration, thermal or noise reports. The agent or the yard arranges ISPS passes and books launches, subject to weather. Ship particulars and likely Malta stops reach us at info@atlantisndt.com, and the enquiry form here does the same job.

faqs.q: Is a CVIP programme in Malta the same as CAS or CAP?
faqs.a: In method it is close to both, and Malta managers borrow the names for that reason. In standing it is different: the owner commissions it and keeps the results, and it carries neither a flag Statement of Compliance nor a classification society rating. If a charterer requires the class CAP, book it with the ship's society; the programme shows the probable result before the survey.

faqs.q: What can be done while a ship bunkers at Hurd's Bank?
faqs.a: Usually machinery and switchboards under port load, deck plating and fittings, hatch covers, scrubber lines and ballast tanks the crew has ventilated and released, provided the weather allows a safe transfer with equipment. Work close to the bunker manifold waits until the transfer is over. Anything that does not fit moves to the next stop in the plan, which may be the Freeport, a terminal or a docking.

faqs.q: Does the flag of a Malta-registered ship change the programme?
faqs.a: No. The programme's method and report format are the same whatever the flag or class. What the Malta flag often brings is a technical department on the island, so the manager can attend a Grand Harbour docking visit and settle priorities with the team directly. Statutory surveys and class gauging remain with the recognised organisation acting for the flag.

faqs.q: Can a programme cover a cruise ship that turns around in Valletta?
faqs.a: Yes. Turnaround days at the Valletta Cruise Port suit machinery readings, thermal surveys of switchboards and hot surfaces, and wall-thickness readings on exhaust gas cleaning pipework at fixed points. Hull, sea chests and scrubber shell outlets are recorded when the ship docks for refurbishment at Palumbo Malta Shipyard, so the turnaround visits and the docking build one record.

faqs.q: Can programme visits in Malta be combined with ships in Sicily or southern Italy?
faqs.a: Often. A Schengen visa covers Malta and Italy, and Sicily is a short flight or ferry crossing away. If a Malta-managed fleet has a ship docking in Grand Harbour and another calling at Palermo or Naples, the visits can be sequenced on one mobilisation, with each ship keeping its own report and trend record.

faqs.q: What does a lender or buyer gain from a Malta programme?
faqs.a: A record that shows direction, not a single date. After several visits the owner can present corrosion rates at numbered points, coating ratings over time, crack findings with their repairs, and machinery trends. Lenders reviewing a fleet and buyers inspecting a ship can work from that history, and because the data files belong to the owner, they can pass to a new owner with the ship.
